items.content:
A former Apple engineer texted a colleague right after he quit:
 
"LOL, I found out I can still access the servers. So funny."
 
That text is now Exhibit A in the biggest tech lawsuit of the year.
 
Last week Apple sued OpenAI. The claim: OpenAI didn't just recruit Apple's people, it recruited what was in their heads, their laptops, and in one case their still-active server login.
 
The filing is wild:
400+ former Apple employees now work at OpenAI.
Its hardware chief allegedly told Apple candidates to bring "actual parts" and prototypes to interviews for "show and tell."
One engineer allegedly kept his Apple laptop and pulled dozens of files on unreleased products after his last day.
OpenAI allegedly passed around an internal Apple guide on how to dodge Apple's own exit-security check.
 
OpenAI denies all of it. A court will decide.
 
But strip the names off and this is a story every founder is living in miniature.
 
I run a business whose entire product is know-how. Clay builds, signal stacks, the whole system on outbounds, ads and content. All of it is, in theory, stealable. People see it, learn it, and some of them leave.
 
For a while I thought the fix was locking it down hard with tighter contracts, more NDAs, guard the playbook.
 
It doesn't work. Apple has the best lawyers on earth, and its unreleased roadmap still allegedly walked out on a personal laptop.
 
Here's what I believe after 3 years of this:
 
The secret was never the moat, the moat is how fast you can make today's secret irrelevant.
 
Apple's edge was never one metal-finishing trick. It was decades of compounding execution that outruns whatever leaks. One AI release can dissolve a "protected" advantage overnight. Speed can't be poached.
 
In our case, we stopped trying to own information and started trying to out-run the copy.
Publish the playbook. Give away the signals. Move faster than anyone who screenshots them.
 
What are you still trying to protect that you'd be better off just giving away?
 
P.S. Flashback to 2024, when Apple and OpenAI shook hands on the partnership Elon Musk immediately mocked. Two years later, they're in court.

Opus 5 dropped last Friday and it halved what near-top AI costs to run.
It gets close to Fable 5, Anthropic's flagship, for $5 and $25 per million tokens, half of Fable 5's $10 and $50.
 
One number got buried under the price cut. AutomationBench, 26%.
That's multi-step business-workflow automation, and Opus 5 beats the whole field by roughly 1.5x, its widest win on the board.

→ For outbound that means an agent can finally run the ops end to end. Stitch funding plus hiring plus tech-stack, tier the account, route it, drive the sending tool, triage the reply. It runs computer use at 70.6% too (OSWorld, #1) for about a third of Fable 5's cost, so it can operate the CRM and internal tools that never shipped a clean API.
 
Across the flywheel, every step that used to be a human handoff gets re-priced with the effort dial. Research 200 newly-funded AI accounts overnight on the low setting for pennies. Long-tail copy, low effort. Reserve max effort for the 20 dream accounts, the offer itself, and the one reply that's mid-negotiation.
 
But cheaper (and better) agents don't fix a bad list.
 
They just let you reach the wrong people faster and more convincingly. Point this at 8,000 rows where 60% are mis-ICP'd and you've sent 5,000 specific, WRONG emails, torching your sending domain on the way.
When personalization costs nothing, the bottleneck moves off execution and onto the list itself. The hard part is knowing which 1,200 of those 8,000 are worth sending, and whether what you'd say about them is even true.

So the first thing I'd rebuild is the list and the offer under it, before touching the outreach at all. Tighten the ICP, kill the dead rows, enrich what's left, then turn the dial to max on the accounts that survive.

items.content:
Building a product is now the easy part.
Getting anyone to use it is the hard part.
 
Before AI, a few people had the idea, some built it, and a massive crowd used it. Usage was the wide end of the funnel. Distribution was mostly free: a good product sold itself. Ship something decent and people found you.
 
After AI, that funnel is upside down.
 
ChatGPT makes everyone's idea sound worth building. Anyone can ship it in a weekend. And almost none of it gets used.
 
Ideas went from scarce to infinite. Code went from months to an afternoon. The one thing that stayed brutally hard: getting a real human to pick you, pay you, and stay.
 
This is why I keep saying GTM is the new MVP.
 
We ran outbound for 275+ companies. The pattern was consistent, and a little painful to admit: the winners had the sharpest motion: right list, right offer, relevant enough that the reply felt obvious. Product quality barely predicted who made it.
 
Frontal is at ~$350k/mo, and the software is not the reason. Someone could clone your tech stack. Nobody clones 100 meetings a month, or the distribution engine that prints them.
 
So here is the uncomfortable math for founders:
 
Your product is a commodity the day after you launch.
Your distribution is the only thing that compounds.
 
Spend the next month on the motion, not the roadmap.
 
♻️ Repost this if you're building something and underneath it fear the product was the easy part.

The average GTM engineer is about to get wiped out. The best one is about to get rich.

This role is going through exactly what software engineering went through in the 2010s.

Back then Silicon Valley had the 10x engineer: one person who did the work of ten. The same gap is opening in GTM right now.

A GTM engineer builds the systems that find leads and run a sales team's outreach. The routine half of that already runs on its own. AI researches the accounts, drafts the outreach, and keeps the follow-ups moving overnight.

So the job is splitting into two.

One version just runs the tools. Anyone with the same setup gets the same output, which means an agent gets there too. Most of those people will end up running their agents inside Claude Code or Codex, and whoever only operates the stack gets cheaper every year.

The other version builds the tools: the agents and the internal systems the rest of the team runs on. That's the person doing the work of ten, and you can't buy it off the shelf. Those roles already pay $40 to $60K above an equivalent RevOps hire, and that gap only widens.

People keep telling me this role is about to dissolve into every other seat. I don't buy it, and 9 in 10 people doing the work don't either. It doesn't disappear. It concentrates: fewer engineers, each one worth far more.

If I were hiring for this today, I'd stop counting the tools someone has used and start looking at the systems they've built.

One of them is about to be worth 10 of the other.

Your content is only as credible as what you're operating right now. The day you stop running the business, the content you make starts to be more and more high level. Your best stories start to be things you did a while ago, and people can feel it fast.

Running a business is the best source material, and I haven't found a better way.

items.content:
Turn the people engaging with your LinkedIn posts into booked meetings.

Here's the 7-step workflow that got our team 120 meetings last month.

1/ Post for your ICP

We use Taplio to spot trending topics before we write, and to see which of our own posts pull the most attention. Then we double down on what's working.

2/ Pull everyone who engaged.

Someone who reacts to a post about outbound automation is telling you what they care about. We use Apify to export a clean list of every profile that liked, commented, or reposted.


3/ Enrich the list in Clay.

We push the list into Clay and layer in company, role, seniority, and firmographics. Now it's a real prospecting dataset instead of a list of names.

4/ Score and tier by ICP fit.

Not everyone who engages is a buyer. We rank each account in Clay. 
Tier 1 is a strong match on role, company size, and industry. Tier 2 and 3 fit, but with lower urgency. 
This keeps us from burning touches on people who were never going to buy.

5/ Find verified emails with a waterfall.

We run the enrichment in sequence inside Clay: Wiza, then Prospeo, then LeadMagic, then FullEnrich. 
If one tool misses the email, the next one catches it. Coverage stays high and you never overpay a single provider.

6/ Add buying signals before you write anything.

This is where relevance comes from. Before reaching out, we pull live context in Clay: active hiring, tech stack, team growth. 
A company hiring SDRs is a completely different conversation than one that isn't.

7/ Reach out based on tier.

Tier 1 gets a LinkedIn DM through Instantly.ai or Expandi, more personal and higher intent. 
Tier 2 and 3 get an email sequence through Instantly, scaled but still personalized with the signals from step 6.

The one rule we never break: no pitch on the first touch. We open with something useful instead, a relevant lead magnet, a quick insight, or the results we got for a similar company. We show we understand their situation before we ask for anything.

Engagement is just the top of the funnel. This workflow is how you turn it into pipeline.

How are you working the people who engage with your posts?

AI works. It was just never going to run the whole thing on its own.

We've run outbound for 276+ companies now. We use the same rule on every one. I call it 10-80-10.

You own the first 10%. Who we go after, what a good lead looks like, the angle to take. That's judgment, and no model makes that call for you. It's also the part people often skip.

AI runs the middle 80%. The research, the data, the first drafts, the follow-ups. Hundreds of accounts in a night, across the tools you already pay for. We build our own software on top so it keeps getting better at that 80%.

Then you own the last 10%. You read the work before a prospect ever does. You catch what the model got wrong, cut what's weak, and decide what goes out.

We've never let an agent run a play end to end. There's always a human on both ends of it.

I don't think AI is coming for your team. I think it makes a good team faster, and it does close to nothing for a team that couldn't tell good work from bad in the first place.

Once AI can do the 80% for everyone, doing the work stops being the edge. The 20% that decides what's worth chasing and what's good enough to send becomes the whole game.

That 20% is what clients pay us for. It's the reason this still needs people.

Demand Planning Mistake: Treating Last Year as the Future!!
One common forecasting mistake is assuming last year will repeat itself.
It rarely does.
Last year’s sales data is useful, but it only tells us:
• What happened?
• Not always why it happened?
• Not always whether the same pattern will happen again?
A planner may say:
“Last Season we sold 15,000 units, so this year we should plan the same.”
But this year may be different.
🔸 Prices changed
🔸 Competitors launched promotions
🔸 Customers shifted behavior
🔸 Supplier lead times changed
🔸 Some SKUs had availability issues
🔸 Sales focus moved to another category
So the forecast may look logical, but still fail.
The problem is not using historical data.
The problem is using historical data without challenging the assumptions.
📊 A Simple Example
Last year’s demand: 15,000 units
This year’s actual demand: 10,500 units
Forecast gap: 4,500 units
Why did the gap happen?
⚠️ Competitor promotion
⚠️ Price increase
⚠️ Supplier delays
⚠️ Customer shift to cheaper alternatives
⚠️ Different sales priorities
The forecast missed because the business copied the past instead of reading the present.
✅ Better Approach
Use history as a baseline, not the final answer.
Before finalizing the forecast, ask:
• What changed in the market?
• Were last year’s sales affected by promotions or stockouts?
• Are customers behaving differently?
• Are competitors influencing demand?
• Do sales, supply, procurement, and finance agree on the assumptions?
Good demand planning is not about copying last year.
It is about:
🔹 Understanding the past
🔹 Reading current signals
🔹 Preparing for what may happen next
The best planners do not ask only:
“What did we sell last year?”
They ask:
“What changed since then?”

Demand Sensing: Using Real-Time Signals Before It’s Too Late!!
Most forecast issues don’t happen because planners ignored data.
They happen because the business reacted too late.
Traditional forecasting often asks:  “What happened last month?”
Demand sensing asks:  “What is demand starting to do now?”
That difference matters.
Because markets move faster than monthly planning cycles.
Demand can shift when:
🔹 Customers change buying behavior
🔹 Competitors launch promotions
🔹 Online demand suddenly spikes
🔹 Supplier delays affect availability
🔹 Sales teams notice early market signals
🔹 Warehouse dispatches increase before reports are reviewed
📊 A Simple Example
Forecast: 20,000 units
But early in the month:
⚠️ Competitor goes out of stock
⚠️ Online searches increase
⚠️ Retailers order more
⚠️ Sales reports faster movement
⚠️ Warehouse dispatches rise
Potential demand moves toward: 28,000 units
If the team waits until month-end, the result may be:
❌ Stockouts
❌ Lost sales
❌ Expediting cost
❌ Emergency procurement
❌ Poor customer service
The issue is not only forecast accuracy.
The issue is weak demand sensing.
🔍 What to Monitor
Demand sensing works when planners connect signals such as:
📦 Sales orders
🛒 POS data
💻 E-commerce demand
⏳ Backorders
📞 Customer inquiries
📢 Promotion plans
🏁 Competitor activity
💰 Market pricing
🚚 Supplier delays
🌍 Logistics disruptions
The goal is not to chase every signal.
The goal is to identify which signals matter for each product category.
✅ Better Approach
Use demand sensing practically:
🔹 Segment SKUs using ABC/XYZ
🔹 Track early demand deviation
🔹 Connect sales, inventory, procurement, and logistics data
🔹 Use exception-based planning
🔹 Validate changes through S&OP
🔹 Apply DMAIC when the same signals are repeatedly missed
Demand sensing is not only about technology.
📊 Dashboards can detect signals.
🤝 Alignment turns signals into decisions.
Demand sensing does not replace forecasting.
It improves the forecast before it becomes outdated.
The best planners do not only explain forecast error after it happens.
They detect demand change early enough to act.

items.content:
Most processes don’t slow down everywhere!
They slow down at one critical point: The bottleneck.
A bottleneck is the step that limits the speed, capacity, or output of the entire process.
In supply chain and operations, bottlenecks often appear as:
🔴 Queue buildup
🔴 Long waiting time
🔴 High utilization but low output
🔴 Repeated expediting
🔴 Rework loops
🔴 Downstream teams waiting
How to identify it?
✅ Map the full process flow
✅ Measure cycle time at each step
✅ Check where work piles up
✅ Compare demand vs capacity
✅ Observe the process at Gemba
✅ Use Pareto analysis to find the biggest delay drivers
Example:
A procurement team may think buyers are the problem.
But data may show the real bottleneck is approval waiting time.
So instead of pushing people harder, the solution could be:
✔ Clear approval matrix
✔ Delegation rules
✔ Escalation triggers
✔ Dashboard visibility
Lean Six Sigma insight:
Don’t optimize every step equally.
First fix the step that controls the flow.
Then check where the next bottleneck appears.
The fastest way to improve a process is not always to work harder.
It is to find what is slowing everything down.
Where do you see the biggest bottleneck in your process — approvals, systems, people, suppliers, or data?

items.content:
Root Cause Analysis: 5 Whys vs Fishbone Diagram
Most quality problems come back because we fix the symptom, not the root cause. 🔁
A defect happens.
A machine stops.
A customer complains.
A shipment is delayed.
The quick reaction is usually:
✅ Rework it
✅ Replace it
✅ Expedite it
✅ Apologize
✅ Close the complaint
But if the root cause is still there, the problem will return.
That is where Root Cause Analysis helps. 🔍
Two simple but powerful tools are:
1️⃣ 5 Whys
Use 5 Whys when the problem has a clear path.
Example: Packaging damaged
➡️ Why 1: Carton was damaged
➡️ Why 2: Packaging was too weak
➡️ Why 3: Wrong specification was used
➡️ Why 4: Old product spec was copied
➡️ Why 5: No packaging validation checklist existed
🎯 Root cause: Missing validation process.
5 Whys helps you go deeper.
2️⃣ Fishbone Diagram
Use Fishbone when there are many possible causes. 🐟
It helps you analyze the issue across the 6M categories:
👷 Manpower — training, fatigue, skill gap
⚙️ Machine — calibration, breakdown, maintenance
📦 Material — supplier variation, wrong specification
📋 Method — unclear SOP, no checklist, poor standard work
📏 Measurement — wrong gauge, late detection, missing data
🌡️ Environment — dust, temperature, layout, lighting
Fishbone helps you see the bigger picture before jumping to conclusions.
Best Practice 🧠
Don’t choose only one.
Use them together:
Fishbone → Pareto → 5 Whys → Corrective Action → Control Plan
Because the goal is not to blame people.
The goal is to improve the process. ⚙️
A label defect may look like operator error.
But the real cause may be:
❌ No setup checklist
❌ No calibration standard
❌ Poor changeover control
❌ Weak training process
❌ Missing first-piece approval
RCA is not a blame exercise.
It is a process improvement discipline.
And when quality improves, the whole supply chain improves. 🚚
Because quality issues do not stay in the factory.
They move into:
📦 Inventory
🗓️ Planning
🚛 Logistics
🎧 Customer service
💰 Cost
⭐ Brand reputation

items.content:
The cheapest supplier is not always the safest supplier.
In procurement, choosing suppliers only by price can create hidden risk.
A low-cost supplier can quickly become expensive when they cause:
❌ Late deliveries
❌ Quality issues
❌ Emergency freight
❌ Stockouts
❌ Production delays
❌ Customer complaints
That’s where the Kraljic Matrix helps.
It classifies suppliers based on two factors:
📌 Profit Impact
How much does the item affect cost, margin, or operations?
📌 Supply Risk
How difficult is it to source if the supplier fails?
The matrix gives 4 supplier categories:
🔴 Strategic Items
High profit impact + high supply risk
➡️ Build partnerships, backup plans, and risk monitoring.
🟠 Bottleneck Items
Low profit impact + high supply risk
➡️ Increase safety stock and qualify alternate suppliers.
🟢 Leverage Items
High profit impact + low supply risk
➡️ Use competition, negotiation, and volume consolidation.
🔵 Routine Items
Low profit impact + low supply risk
➡️ Automate, simplify, and reduce manual effort.
The key lesson?
Procurement should not ask only:
“Which supplier is cheapest?”
Procurement should also ask:
“What happens if this supplier fails?”
Because supplier selection is not just about saving money.
It is about protecting cost, continuity, and customer service.
Right classification. Right strategy. Lower risk. Higher value.

Forecast Bias: The Silent Planning Error!
Forecast error tells you how much you missed.
Forecast bias tells you whether you keep missing in the same direction.
That difference matters.
When forecasts are consistently too high, the result is:
📦 Excess inventory
⏳ Aging stock
💰 Cash blocked
🏷️ Markdown pressure
🏭 Warehouse congestion
When forecasts are consistently too low, the result is:
🚫 Stockouts
📉 Lost sales
🚚 Emergency buying
❌ Poor OTIF
🤝 Lost customer trust
A forecast can look “acceptable” on accuracy reports but still damage the business if it keeps leaning high or low.
That is why demand planning teams should track bias separately from accuracy.
Forecast Bias % = (Σ Forecast − Σ Actual) ÷ Σ Actual × 100
Positive bias = over-forecasting
Negative bias = under-forecasting
Near zero = balanced planning
To tackle forecast bias:
✅ Compare statistical forecast vs sales input vs final forecast
✅ Clean demand history from stockouts, promotions, bulk orders, and abnormal demand
✅ Review bias by SKU, customer, category, and region
✅ Set bias control limits
✅ Discuss bias monthly in S&OP
Forecast bias is not just a planning metric.
It is a warning signal that business assumptions are drifting from reality.
The best teams do not only ask:
“How accurate were we?”
They also ask:
“Are we consistently wrong in the same direction?”
What do you see more often in your organization — over-forecasting or under-forecasting?

items.content:
Cost Avoidance: The Procurement Achievement That Often Goes Unnoticed!
In procurement, everyone celebrates cost savings.
✅ Negotiated 5% discount
✅ Reduced supplier price
✅ Consolidated spend
✅ Lowered purchase cost
These are easy to see.
But one of the most valuable procurement contributions is often ignored:
Cost Avoidance.
Cost avoidance is the cost increase that procurement prevents before it hits the business.
It may not always appear as direct savings in the P&L.
But it protects margin, budget, continuity, and customer service.
Examples of cost avoidance in procurement:
🛡️ Preventing a supplier price increase
📦 Avoiding emergency freight by planning early
🌍 Reducing tariff exposure through alternate sourcing
📉 Avoiding material cost escalation through fixed-price contracts
🏭 Preventing production downtime by qualifying backup suppliers
✅ Avoiding quality failures through better supplier evaluation
⏱️ Reducing delay risk through improved lead-time agreements
💰 Avoiding extra inventory cost through better MOQ negotiation
The challenge?
Cost avoidance is often invisible.
When procurement prevents a problem, people may not notice because the crisis never happened.
But that does not mean value was not created.
In fact, preventing cost is sometimes more powerful than reducing cost.
Because cost savings improve today’s numbers.
But cost avoidance protects tomorrow’s business.
Procurement should not only report:
“We saved this much.”
Procurement should also report:
“We prevented this much cost exposure.”
For example:
A supplier announces a 12% price increase.
Procurement negotiates, validates market data, reviews alternate suppliers, and limits the increase to 4%.
The visible saving may not look dramatic.
But the avoided cost is real.
That 8% prevented increase is a procurement achievement.
The same applies to avoiding:
❌ Stockouts
❌ Expedite charges
❌ Supplier failure
❌ Rework cost
❌ Contract leakage
❌ Tariff impact
❌ Poor payment terms
❌ Unplanned price escalation
In today’s volatile supply chain environment, procurement is not just a buying function.
It is a value protection function.
The best procurement teams do not only chase discounts.
They protect the business from hidden cost exposure.
Cost saving gets attention.
Cost avoidance deserves recognition.
Because the best cost is often the one your business never had to pay.

SAFETY STOCK

🛡️📦 Safety Stock is not excess inventory — it’s protection against uncertainty.
Demand fluctuations, supplier delays, and lead time variability can disrupt operations. Safety stock acts as a buffer to maintain service levels and business continuity.

A well-managed safety stock strategy helps:

✔ Prevent stockouts
✔ Improve customer satisfaction
✔ Reduce supply chain disruptions
✔ Balance inventory cost & service level
✔ Support operational stability

The goal is simple:

👉 Right inventory
👉 Right quantity
👉 Right time

How does your organization calculate safety stock — statistical model, ERP settings, or planner experience?
